title: Live the book
hookLine: proud of explaining Chrysippus? better to live what he wrote, and keep your principles like laws (Enchiridion 49–50)

lines: THE GYM EXPERT WHO NEVER LIFTS.
cards: There's a kind of person you meet at the gym. They know everything about protein timing, muscle fibers, the right angle for every lift, and they'll explain it to you at length. They rarely lift.
Philosophy has the same person, and so do plenty of hobbies: the one who can explain the book better than anyone, and whose life looks nothing like it.
In Epictetus' school, the books students were proud to explain were by Chrysippus. Section forty-nine takes aim at the explainers.

teach.b: Chrysippus was the third head of the Stoic school, and the ancient biographers say he wrote more than seven hundred works.
Epictetus' own joke implies he was hard to read, so a student who could explain him felt rather proud.
When someone boasts of that, Epictetus says, tell yourself: if Chrysippus had written clearly, this man would have nothing to boast about. Then he walks it through. What do I want?
To understand nature and follow it. I find out Chrysippus explains it. I can't follow him, so I find someone who can explain Chrysippus.
So far, nothing to be proud of.
Explaining is only the doorway. What's left is to put the teaching into practice, and that alone is something to be proud of.
If all I admire is the explaining, I'm a grammarian, not a philosopher, explaining Chrysippus instead of Homer.

teach.h: I BLUSH WHEN MY ACTIONS DON'T MATCH.
teach.b: And when someone asks me to read Chrysippus to them, I blush, because I can't show actions that match the words. The next section turns it into a rule.
Whatever principles you've taken on, keep them like laws, as if breaking them would be a kind of sacrilege.
And whatever people say about you, pay no attention; that isn't yours. So the fair question isn't how much you can explain. It's which one line you're actually living.

how: Some people practicing Stoicism choose a single principle from their reading and try to act on it for a day, rather than reading or explaining more.

o: the founder of the Stoic school in Athens
the Stoic writer whose books students loved to explain
Epictetus' teacher, who said to live the book

games.q: live the book — tap the pairs.
p: third head of the Stoic school

s: Chrysippus is said to have written over seven hundred works
so the ancient biographer Diogenes Laertius reports.
Epictetus says being able to explain Chrysippus is the goal
it's the doorway. the goal is actions that match the words.

games.q: a fellow student asks you to read and explain Chrysippus to him. how does Epictetus say he feels?
o: proud to show what he knows.
he blushes, when he can't show actions that match the words.
games.why: explaining is no achievement. what he'd be proud of is living it, and he blushes when his actions fall short.

practice: Let one line rise up from this path, or from any book that has mattered to you, the one that's stuck: maybe two handles, maybe wait, maybe something older. Say it to yourself once.
Then picture one ordinary moment where you live it instead of explaining it, in plain clothes, in an ordinary room.

wordCard.voice: Chrysippus. The Stoic writer whose books were hard to explain; explaining him is only the doorway, what counts is actions that match the words. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: explanation, interpretation. Enchiridion 49 uses the related verb.

carryVoice: Your line: actions that match the words. Explaining is the doorway, not the room. Back tomorrow.
